questions.title: Did § 1216’s “shall … conduct an investigation” obligate OSC here, independent of FOIA § 552(a)(4)(F)(i)?
questions.question_body: The district court said § 552(a)(4)(F)(i)’s three predicates (court order, fee award, and specific finding about arbitrariness) don’t limit OSC’s power under § 1216(a)(3), but the D.C. Circuit didn’t reach the merits. How should these provisions be read together? Does § 1216(a)(3) impose a nondiscretionary duty to investigate upon any allegation of an “arbitrary or capricious withholding” under FOIA, or is there some threshold? If the duty is nondiscretionary, what is the proper vehicle to enforce it—APA § 706(1) or mandamus?

questions.title: Why isn’t DOJ’s failure to produce records a traceable, redressable informational injury caused by OSC’s refusal to investigate?
questions.question_body: AFL argued that OSC’s refusal to investigate DOJ under § 1216 ultimately kept AFL from getting FOIA records. The panel said the injury is traceable to DOJ, not OSC, and that the chain through possible OSC action, MSPB sanctions, and DOJ compliance is too speculative (citing Haaland v. Brackeen and FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine). Can someone clarify how these cases limit causation/redressability when a plaintiff sues a regulator for not enforcing against a third party? Are there examples where a regulator’s inaction has been held sufficiently traceable/redressable despite intervening independent actors?

questions.title: Does § 1216(c)’s “in the same way as if a prohibited personnel practice were involved” language import § 1214’s notice rights?
questions.question_body: AFL claimed an informational injury from not receiving the investigation notices and updates that § 1214 provides. The panel says § 1216 doesn’t itself entitle requesters to information and cites Carson v. OSC for the idea that applying § 1214 procedures in § 1216 investigations is discretionary. How do courts interpret § 1216(c)’s cross-reference—does it incorporate only the remedial avenues (corrective under § 1214 and disciplinary under § 1215), or also § 1214’s procedural notice requirements to complainants? If some § 1214 procedures do carry over, which ones and on what rationale?

questions.title: What exactly is relaxed in procedural-injury standing, and why didn’t it help AFL here?
questions.question_body: The opinion quotes D.C. Circuit precedent that imminence and redressability are relaxed for procedural injuries, but injury in fact and causation are not. Yet it finds AFL’s first theory fails on causation and redressability, and its second theory lacks a statutory entitlement (injury) and redressability. In practice, what does the relaxed standard permit (e.g., probabilistic chains)? Where is the line between acceptable probability and impermissible speculation about “independent actors not before the court”?

questions.title: Could AFL have pled organizational standing (resource diversion) based on OSC’s refusal to investigate?
questions.question_body: AFL’s supplemental briefing focused on informational/procedural injuries. Under D.C. Circuit organizational-standing doctrine, could AFL have alleged a concrete resource-diversion injury—e.g., that OSC’s non-investigation forced AFL to divert staff time and money to counteract DOJ’s email-search policy—traceable to OSC and redressable by a court order? What specific factual allegations would be needed to satisfy injury, causation, and redressability on that theory?

questions.title: After finding no standing, why did the D.C. Circuit vacate the merits ruling and remand with instructions to dismiss?
questions.question_body: The district court held OSC made a legal error about its authority but still declined to order an investigation, and it remanded to OSC. The court of appeals vacated because there was no Article III standing. Is vacatur of the merits ruling automatic when jurisdiction is lacking (per Steel Co.)? Do the district court’s legal conclusions about § 1216 and § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) have any continuing effect, or are they null once vacated?

questions.title: If standing were satisfied, could a court compel OSC to investigate under § 1216, or would Heckler v. Chaney bar that relief?
questions.question_body: The district court suggested decisions under § 1216(c) are committed to OSC’s discretion. Chaney generally bars review of nonenforcement, while Norton v. SUWA allows courts to compel discrete, nondiscretionary agency actions. Would a § 1216(a)(3) “shall … conduct an investigation” duty be enforceable under APA § 706(1) or mandamus, and if so, would the remedy be limited to initiating an investigation (as opposed to dictating outcomes or enforcement actions)?

questions.title: Does a DOJ policy of not searching employee emails without consent qualify as an “arbitrary or capricious withholding” under FOIA for § 1216 purposes?
questions.question_body: Section 1216(a)(3) covers “arbitrary or capricious withholding of information prohibited under section 552.” Is a systemic search-limitation policy (not searching certain repositories absent employee consent) properly characterized as a FOIA “withholding,” or does that term refer only to refusing to disclose located records based on exemptions? How, if at all, have courts or OSC treated search-adequacy issues in the context of § 552(a)(4)(F) referrals or § 1216 investigations?
